title: COFF — Common Object File Format
description: Read a COFF object file: its file header, its section table, and the symbol and relocation records a linker uses to place code whose final address nobody knows yet.
author: Underlayer
completion_criteria: Decode a COFF object file end to end, resolve every name through the string table, and explain what a relocation asks the linker to do.

concepts.title: Why COFF Exists
concepts.description: The link step, what relocatable means, and why a COFF object cannot be executed.

concepts.title: The File Header
concepts.description: All seven fields of IMAGE_FILE_HEADER, and how Machine tells you the pointer width.

concepts.title: The Section Header
concepts.description: Ten fields in forty bytes, and the section that reserves four bytes it does not contain.

concepts.title: Section Characteristics
concepts.description: The flags the linker obeys, and why alignment is a four-bit field that seven bitmask tests get wrong at once.

concepts.title: The String Table
concepts.description: The pool every long name resolves through, and the three different encodings that can point into it.

concepts.title: The Symbol Table
concepts.description: The 18-byte symbol, storage classes, and an aux record whose field order is not the documented one.

concepts.title: Relocations
concepts.description: Ten bytes per unanswered question, the AMD64 type table, and the packed layout the compiler does not emit.

concepts.title: COMDAT and Duplicate Sections
concepts.description: How a linker is told which of two identical sections to keep, why the checksum can differ, and how the dialects differ.

concepts.title: bigobj
concepts.description: The over-65,535 variant whose header relocates its fields rather than widening them, and the 0x0000FFFF signature it shares with short-import libraries.

concepts.title: The .lib Archive
concepts.description: The ar container a .lib is: the 8-byte magic, the 60-byte member header with its decimal size field, and the two symbol indexes that use different byte orders.

concepts.title: Line Numbers
concepts.description: The two section-header fields that are always zero, the 6-byte record layout verified by construction, and why the values mean nothing before the link.

concepts.title: The Link
concepts.description: A real COFF-to-PE link, watched step by step: sections given addresses, four zero bytes becoming a displacement, and sections dropped by flags read out of the header.

concepts.title: Map Files
concepts.description: The linker's plain-text transcript: the discard list, the memory configuration, the linker-defined symbols, and the *fill* rows that account for 15 of 69 bytes of .text.

concepts.title: COMDAT in the Linker
concepts.description: COMDAT deduplication observed working end to end, and a reproduced silent miscompilation: two different function bodies, one checksum, and a linker that discarded the wrong one.

concepts.title: ARM64 Relocations
concepts.description: A real ARM64 object: five relocation types from four functions, the two-instruction pairs that only make sense together, and a 26-bit branch field that must be range-checked.

concepts.title: Thread Local Storage
concepts.description: The .tls$ section: characteristics byte-identical to .data, contents that are a template rather than the variables, and a link that cannot be completed on this machine.

concepts.title: Weak Externals
concepts.description: A third symbol state: storage class 105, the auxiliary record that names a fallback, and a branch in the generated code as the observable cost.

concepts.title: Linker Directives in a Section
concepts.description: A section whose contents are instructions to the linker: 23 bytes decoded, and observed being discarded with a controlled comparison as the control.

exercise_decls.question: Without looking back: a member header reports size = 16. How many bytes of member body follow, and what does the next member header start at relative to this one?
exercise_decls.answer: 16 bytes of body, and the next header is 76 bytes further on — 60 for this header plus 16 for the body. Sixteen is even, so no pad byte is needed
exercise_decls.options: 16 bytes of body, and the next header is 76 bytes further on — 60 for this header plus 16 for the body. Sixteen is even, so no pad byte is needed|22 bytes of body, because the size field is hexadecimal, so the next header is 82 bytes further on|17 bytes of body, because an odd-sized member is always followed by one pad byte to keep the next header aligned
exercise_decls.explanation: The size field is decimal, so sixteen bytes of body, and the next header begins 60 + 16 = 76 bytes on. The parity rule would not add a pad byte here because 16 is already even. Had the size been 15, the next header would still be even-aligned and a single pad byte would sit between the body and the next header, putting the next header at 60 + 15 + 1.
exercise_decls.hint1: Re-read the lesson section 'Check Your Understanding'.
exercise_decls.source_quote: 16 bytes of body, and the next header is 76 bytes further on — 60 for this header plus 16 for the body. Sixteen is even, so no pad byte is needed

exercise_decls.question: Without looking back: an object has relocations at 0x00 and 0x04, both naming the same symbol — the first IMAGE_REL_ARM64_PAGEBASE_REL21, the second IMAGE_REL_ARM64_PAGEOFFSET_12L. The instruction at 0x2000; after linking, the symbol is at 0x3008. What goes in each field, and why must a relocator treat the two entries as one operation rather than two?
exercise_decls.answer: The page field gets +1 (the page-number difference) and the offset field gets 0x008. They are two halves of one address, so a relocator that applies or validates them independently has a value that is a valid page number and a valid offset belonging to no particular page
exercise_decls.options: The page field gets +1 (the page-number difference) and the offset field gets 0x008. They are two halves of one address, so a relocator that applies or validates them independently has a value that is a valid page number and a valid offset belonging to no particular page|The page field gets 0x1000 and the offset field gets 3, because the 12-bit field holds the page number and the 21-bit field holds the offset within the page|The page field gets +1 and the offset field gets 0x008, but no 21-bit value can represent a page delta of +1, so the linker must report a range error
exercise_decls.explanation: The two fields carry different halves of one address and neither is meaningful alone. The page-base field gets the signed difference of the two page numbers, which here is 3 minus 2, so plus one page, and it is stored in 21 signed bits so the value stays position-independent and small. The page-offset field gets the low twelve bits of the target, 0x008, unsigned. The two must be applied as a unit because each is only half the address: read the page field alone and you have a page number with no offset, read the offset alone and you have an offset into a page you have not identified, and both are valid-looking numbers. The pairing is also why the entry at 0x04 is four bytes after 0x00: the two halves fill two adjacent four-byte instructions.
exercise_decls.hint1: Re-read the lesson section 'Check Your Understanding'.
exercise_decls.source_quote: The page field gets +1 (the page-number difference) and the offset field gets 0x008. They are two halves of one address, so a relocator that applies or validates them independently has a value that is a valid page number and a valid offset belonging to no particular page

exercise_decls.question: Without looking back: a bigobj file is handed to a parser that assumes the classic 20-byte header. It reads Machine as 0 and NumberOfSections as 65535, and no error is raised. Why is that more dangerous than a corrupt classic object, and what single check would have caught it?
exercise_decls.answer: Because every value it reads is a real byte from a real header at the wrong offset, so they are individually plausible — and the fix is to test offset 0 for the 0x0000FFFF signature before parsing anything else
exercise_decls.options: Because every value it reads is a real byte from a real header at the wrong offset, so they are individually plausible — and the fix is to test offset 0 for the 0x0000FFFF signature before parsing anything else|Because SizeOfOptionalHeader would be read as a huge value, which no object can have, so the parser would stop immediately|Because 65535 sections is impossible in practice, so any reader that sanity-checks the section count against the file size would reject it
exercise_decls.explanation: A corrupt classic object usually produces an implausible value somewhere a reader can check: a machine type that does not exist, a section count that runs off the end of the file, a symbol pointer outside the section. A bigobj produces values that are all individually plausible, because they are real bytes from a real header read at the wrong offsets. The one field that cannot be plausible is the two-word signature at offset 0, and it costs a single comparison.
exercise_decls.hint1: Re-read the lesson section 'Check Your Understanding'.
exercise_decls.source_quote: Because every value it reads is a real byte from a real header at the wrong offset, so they are individually plausible — and the fix is to test offset 0 for the 0x0000FFFF signature before parsing anything else

exercise_decls.question: Without looking back: a section header has Characteristics = 0x40300040. Which four flags does it carry, and what is its alignment?
exercise_decls.answer: Read-only initialised data, alignment 3 = ALIGN_4BYTES, and no execute or write bit. This is .xdata
exercise_decls.options: Read-only initialised data, alignment 3 = ALIGN_4BYTES, and no execute or write bit. This is .xdata|It is executable, read-only initialised data, align 3 = ALIGN_4BYTES|It is writable, uninitialised data, align 3 = ALIGN_4BYTES
exercise_decls.explanation: 0x40300040 decomposes as 0x40000000 (MEM_READ) + 0x00300000 (alignment field = 3) + 0x40 (CNT_INITIALIZED_DATA). Alignment 3 is ALIGN_4BYTES. No MEM_EXECUTE and no MEM_WRITE. This is .xdata, the exception-unwinding table, which is read-only initialised data needing 4-byte alignment for its 4-byte fields.
exercise_decls.hint1: Re-read the lesson section 'Check Your Understanding'.
exercise_decls.source_quote: Read-only initialised data, alignment 3 = ALIGN_4BYTES, and no execute or write bit. This is .xdata

exercise_decls.question: Without looking back: a COMDAT section has Selection = 5 (ASSOCIATIVE) and Number = 5, and another COMDAT section has Selection = 5 and Number = 5 as well. What will the linker do with the pair, and why would keeping one of them be a bug?
exercise_decls.answer: It treats them as one group and keeps or discards both together. Keeping one would leave an exception-unwinding record pointing at unwind data that is no longer there, which faults at runtime rather than at link time
exercise_decls.options: It treats them as one group and keeps or discards both together. Keeping one would leave an exception-unwinding record pointing at unwind data that is no longer there, which faults at runtime rather than at link time|It keeps whichever of the two has the matching checksum, since a matching checksum means the contents are identical|It keeps the first one it encounters and discards the second, because equal Numbers mean the sections are duplicates
exercise_decls.explanation: Equal Number plus Selection 5 makes the two sections one group. The linker keeps both or discards both, because a .pdata entry without its .xdata entry points at unwind data that is not there, and the exception unwinder faults. Neither half means anything alone, which is exactly the situation ASSOCIATIVE exists to express - ANY would let the linker keep one and break the program.
exercise_decls.hint1: Re-read the lesson section 'Check Your Understanding'.
exercise_decls.source_quote: It treats them as one group and keeps or discards both together. Keeping one would leave an exception-unwinding record pointing at unwind data that is no longer there, which faults at runtime rather than at link time

exercise_decls.question: Without looking back: two objects each contain a twelve-byte COMDAT .text with Selection: Any and Checksum: 0xF787F24A. The twelve bytes are identical. The linker discards one of them. Now the caller in the discarded object still needs to reach that function. What has to happen, and what would go wrong if the linker simply deleted the section and left the call site alone?
exercise_decls.answer: The call site's relocation must be redirected to the surviving copy in the other object and its displacement recomputed for the new, cross-file distance. Deleting the section alone would leave a fixup pointing into a section that no longer exists, so the call would go to whatever now occupies that address
exercise_decls.options: The call site's relocation must be redirected to the surviving copy in the other object and its displacement recomputed for the new, cross-file distance. Deleting the section alone would leave a fixup pointing into a section that no longer exists, so the call would go to whatever now occupies that address|Nothing needs to change, because the two copies are byte-identical, so every call site that pointed at the discarded copy already computes the right displacement|The symbol is removed from the symbol table, and the linker resolves the call by name at fixup time, so no address needs to be recomputed
exercise_decls.explanation: Discarding a COMDAT section is an alias operation, not a deletion. The caller's REL32 fixup was computed against the discarded copy's address, which was its own section's address, so the linker has to re-point the reference at the survivor and recompute the displacement for the new distance — and the new distance is across object files, so it is not a value anyone had written down. This is why deduplication and relocation have to be coordinated rather than independent passes: a relocation computed against a section that is about to be discarded is wrong the instant the discard happens, and the wrongness is silent because the fixup is still marked applied.
exercise_decls.hint1: Re-read the lesson section 'Check Your Understanding'.
exercise_decls.source_quote: The call site's relocation must be redirected to the surviving copy in the other object and its displacement recomputed for the new, cross-file distance. Deleting the section alone would leave a fixup pointing into a section that no longer exists, so the call would go to whatever now occupies that address

exercise_decls.question: Without looking back: an object has a section .drectve, 23 bytes of contents beginning with a space, and characteristics 0x00100a00. Its SizeOfRawData is 23. The linked image has no section of that name, and the map file lists .drectve 0x00000000 0x17 directive_used.obj among the discarded input sections. What did the linker do with those 23 bytes, and what would have happened if the characteristics had not included IMAGE_SCN_LNK_REMOVE?
exercise_decls.answer: It parsed the option, obeyed it, and discarded the section — the map row is the evidence. Without LNK_REMOVE the 23 bytes would be placed into the image as a section of program data, occupying address space and holding linker text
exercise_decls.options: It parsed the option, obeyed it, and discarded the section — the map row is the evidence. Without LNK_REMOVE the 23 bytes would be placed into the image as a section of program data, occupying address space and holding linker text|It ignored the contents and discarded the section anyway, because IMAGE_SCN_LNK_INFO tells the linker the section is not program data and must not be placed|It would have copied the 23 bytes into the output as a .drectve section, so the option would still be readable in the shipped binary for later auditing
exercise_decls.explanation: Both halves are the concept. The linker read the contents, parsed the option out of the free text, installed the redirection in its symbol resolution, and then discarded the section because LNK_REMOVE was set, which is what the map row records. Without that flag the section would be treated as ordinary data and placed into the output, taking 23 bytes of address space and appearing in the image as a section holding linker text. That is not merely untidy: a section whose declared content is an instruction to the linker would then be present in the program, reachable in principle and meaningless in practice, and the LNK_INFO flag would be the only thing distinguishing it. The two flags together express the section's whole role: information addressed to the linker, and not part of the output.
exercise_decls.hint1: Re-read the lesson section 'Check Your Understanding'.
exercise_decls.source_quote: It parsed the option, obeyed it, and discarded the section — the map row is the evidence. Without LNK_REMOVE the 23 bytes would be placed into the image as a section of program data, occupying address space and holding linker text

exercise_decls.question: Without looking back: NumberOfSymbols is 31 and PointerToSymbolTable is 0x348. Where does the symbol table end, and what begins there?
exercise_decls.answer: At 0x576, and the string table begins there — 31 records of 18 bytes is 558, and 0x348 + 558 = 0x576
exercise_decls.options: At 0x576, and the string table begins there — 31 records of 18 bytes is 558, and 0x348 + 558 = 0x576|At 0x336, because NumberOfSymbols counts names and 31 records of 18 bytes is 246 bytes past 0x348|There is nothing after the symbol table — the section table comes next and then the file ends
exercise_decls.explanation: 31 records of 18 bytes is 558 bytes = 0x22E, so 0x348 + 0x22E = 0x576. The string table follows immediately, and its own first four bytes are its total size, 57, so the file ends exactly at 0x576 + 57 = 1455. Two independent fields agreeing on one boundary is the check.
exercise_decls.hint1: Re-read the lesson section 'Check Your Understanding'.
exercise_decls.source_quote: At 0x576, and the string table begins there — 31 records of 18 bytes is 558, and 0x348 + 558 = 0x576

exercise_decls.question: Without looking back: you are handed a file whose SizeOfOptionalHeader is zero. Can the operating system run it?
exercise_decls.answer: No. There is no entry point and no data directories, because a zero optional header means they are not there. Only a linker can consume it
exercise_decls.options: No. There is no entry point and no data directories, because a zero optional header means they are not there. Only a linker can consume it|Yes. The loader falls back to a default entry point when the optional header is absent|No, but the linker can run it by resolving the relocations at load time
exercise_decls.explanation: A zero SizeOfOptionalHeader means there is no optional header at all, so the file carries no entry point, no image base and no data directories. The OS loader has nothing to work with, and the file instead carries relocations that only a linker can resolve. The OS will reject it as a bad executable format.
exercise_decls.hint1: Re-read the lesson section 'Check Your Understanding'.
exercise_decls.source_quote: No. There is no entry point and no data directories, because a zero optional header means they are not there. Only a linker can consume it

exercise_decls.question: Without looking back: you are writing a tool that lists the source lines covered by a COFF object. Every section reports NumberOfLinenumbers: 0. What is the correct conclusion, and what must you not conclude?
exercise_decls.answer: This toolchain does not write COFF line numbers. The fields are real and correctly located — but you may not conclude the format lacks the feature, or that the object has no debug information at all
exercise_decls.options: This toolchain does not write COFF line numbers. The fields are real and correctly located — but you may not conclude the format lacks the feature, or that the object has no debug information at all|The fields are vestigial. They are present in the section header for historical reasons, no modern producer writes them, and the format has moved on to CodeView entirely|The object is malformed, because a section with a zero line-number count and a zero pointer is internally inconsistent
exercise_decls.explanation: A zero count means this producer did not write COFF line numbers, which is a fact about the toolchain rather than about the file's validity or about the format. The companion field PointerToLinenumbers being zero too is consistent with that. What you must not conclude is that the fields are vestigial or that the object has no debug information at all - the same object carries a .debug$S section of CodeView data, which is a different mechanism the COFF section header has no field for.
exercise_decls.hint1: Re-read the lesson section 'Check Your Understanding'.
exercise_decls.source_quote: This toolchain does not write COFF line numbers. The fields are real and correctly located — but you may not conclude the format lacks the feature, or that the object has no debug information at all

exercise_decls.question: Without looking back: a COFF object has .text with VirtualAddress = 0, four zero bytes at offset 0xe, and a relocation 0xE IMAGE_REL_I386_REL32 _helper. After linking, .text is at 0x1000, the image base is 0x400000, and _helper is at 0x401020. What goes into those four bytes, and what was actually true about the zeros before the link?
exercise_decls.answer: They become 0e 00 00 00 — the displacement 0x401020 - (0x40100d + 5). The zeros were not a wrong value: they were the placeholder for a displacement that did not exist yet, and the relocation entry was the real content of the field
exercise_decls.options: They become 0e 00 00 00 — the displacement 0x401020 - (0x40100d + 5). The zeros were not a wrong value: they were the placeholder for a displacement that did not exist yet, and the relocation entry was the real content of the field|They become the absolute address of _helper, little-endian: 20 10 40 00. That is what an absolute relocation would write, and it is why relative fixups exist|They become 0x20, the section-relative offset of _helper within .text, since a relocatable object addresses everything relative to its own sections|They become ff ff ff f2, the signed difference 0x401020 - 0x40100e measured from the start of the field rather than from the end of the instruction
exercise_decls.explanation: The four bytes become 0x0e, because the call instruction's displacement is measured from the address after the instruction, not from the section start. The zeros in the object were not an unresolved value waiting to be filled in; they were the accurate content of a field whose value genuinely was zero, because at object time the code was at no address and no displacement existed. The relocation entry is what carries the information, and the field is its storage. That is the conceptual heart of a relocatable format: the data is a placeholder and the relocation is the statement of what belongs there.
exercise_decls.hint1: Re-read the lesson section 'Check Your Understanding'.
exercise_decls.source_quote: They become 0e 00 00 00 — the displacement 0x401020 - (0x40100d + 5). The zeros were not a wrong value: they were the placeholder for a displacement that did not exist yet, and the relocation entry was the real content of the field

exercise_decls.question: Without looking back: an output section is declared as 0x200 bytes, and its placement rows account for a 21-byte input section, 11 bytes of filler, a 12-byte input section, 4 bytes of filler, and a 21-byte input section. What is the section's real content size, how much of the declared size is padding, and which of those two numbers does a disassembler see?
exercise_decls.answer: Content is 54 bytes, 15 of the 69 accounted bytes are filler, and 443 of the 512 are tail padding. A disassembler sees only the 54 bytes of code — it decodes instructions and stops at the filler, so the padding is invisible to it
exercise_decls.options: Content is 54 bytes, 15 of the 69 accounted bytes are filler, and 443 of the 512 are tail padding. A disassembler sees only the 54 bytes of code — it decodes instructions and stops at the filler, so the padding is invisible to it|Content is 69 bytes, because the filler rows are part of the section, and 443 bytes are tail padding. A disassembler sees all 69|Content is 512 bytes, the whole declared size, because a section's size in the image includes its padding by definition and the filler is part of it
exercise_decls.explanation: 21 + 12 + 21 is 54 bytes of actual content, 11 + 4 is 15 bytes of linker-inserted filler, and 0x200 minus 69 is 443 bytes of tail padding, so the allocated section is far larger than anything in it. The distinction matters because the three numbers answer different questions and tools report different ones: a disassembler shows you the 54 bytes of code and skips the filler, llvm-readobj's VirtualSize reports the 69, and the map's 0x200 is the allocation rounded to the file alignment. Expecting a section's size to be its code size is the assumption this artifact exists to break.
exercise_decls.hint1: Re-read the lesson section 'Check Your Understanding'.
exercise_decls.source_quote: Content is 54 bytes, 15 of the 69 accounted bytes are filler, and 443 of the 512 are tail padding. A disassembler sees only the 54 bytes of code — it decodes instructions and stops at the filler, so the padding is invisible to it

exercise_decls.question: Without looking back: a .text relocation record reads addr 0x5D, symbol 20, type 4. Which of the three fields is a section-relative offset rather than a file offset or a virtual address, and what does type 4 mean the linker will do?
exercise_decls.answer: It is VirtualAddress, and 0x5D is 93 bytes into .text. Type 4 is REL32: the linker writes a 32-bit relative displacement, target minus the address of the field plus 4
exercise_decls.options: It is VirtualAddress, and 0x5D is 93 bytes into .text. Type 4 is REL32: the linker writes a 32-bit relative displacement, target minus the address of the field plus 4|It is VirtualAddress and it is a file offset, so 0x5D is byte 93 of the file|It is the SymbolTableIndex that is the offset, and type 4 means the linker writes the target's absolute 4-byte address
exercise_decls.explanation: VirtualAddress in a relocation is an offset within the owning section, which is the only frame of reference that means anything before the file is placed. Type 4 is IMAGE_REL_AMD64_REL32, a relative displacement: the linker writes target minus (address of this field plus 4). That is what makes call instructions position-independent within the section.
exercise_decls.hint1: Re-read the lesson section 'Check Your Understanding'.
exercise_decls.source_quote: It is VirtualAddress, and 0x5D is 93 bytes into .text. Type 4 is REL32: the linker writes a 32-bit relative displacement, target minus the address of the field plus 4

exercise_decls.question: Without looking back: a section header reports SizeOfRawData = 4 and PointerToRawData = 0x0. What does the linker do with this section, and where does it find out how big it will finally be?
exercise_decls.answer: It allocates four zero bytes at link time, because a zero pointer with a non-zero size means "implicit zeros". The final size comes from the symbol table's aux record for that section, not from the section header
exercise_decls.options: It allocates four zero bytes at link time, because a zero pointer with a non-zero size means "implicit zeros". The final size comes from the symbol table's aux record for that section, not from the section header|It treats the section as starting at file offset 0 and reads the first four bytes, which is how a section with a null pointer is defined|It reads the size from VirtualSize in the same header, which is 0 here and therefore means the section is empty
exercise_decls.explanation: A zero raw data pointer with a non-zero size means the bytes are implicit zeros. The linker allocates the space and zero-fills it, which is the entire point of .bss: uninitialised globals cost nothing in the object file. The final size is in the section's aux symbol record, where .bss's Length is 4 - not in the section header, whose SizeOfRawData is only a file fact.
exercise_decls.hint1: Re-read the lesson section 'Check Your Understanding'.
exercise_decls.source_quote: It allocates four zero bytes at link time, because a zero pointer with a non-zero size means "implicit zeros". The final size comes from the symbol table's aux record for that section, not from the section header

exercise_decls.question: Without looking back: a symbol's eight-byte name field is 00 00 00 00 1F 00 00 00. What is the symbol called, and how do you get there?
exercise_decls.answer: The first four bytes being zero marks the long-name form; the offset is 0x1F = 31, and string-table offset 31 is ??_C@_03PLHFFLIH@ptr?$AA@
exercise_decls.options: The first four bytes being zero marks the long-name form; the offset is 0x1F = 31, and string-table offset 31 is ??_C@_03PLHFFLIH@ptr?$AA@|The name is empty — an all-zero field means the symbol has no name, which is legal for some aux-only records|The name is stored inline and happens to be 0x1F, the ASCII control character
exercise_decls.explanation: The first four bytes being zero is the signal that this is not an inline name. The next four bytes are a little-endian offset, 0x1f = 31. Add that to the string table's base of 0x576 and read from there: the 25 characters are the MSVC-mangled name of the "ptr" string literal. The inline form simply was not wide enough for it.
exercise_decls.hint1: Re-read the lesson section 'Check Your Understanding'.
exercise_decls.source_quote: The first four bytes being zero marks the long-name form; the offset is 0x1F = 31, and string-table offset 31 is ??_C@_03PLHFFLIH@ptr?$AA@

exercise_decls.question: Without looking back: you are walking the symbol table and reach slot 1. What is there, and what mistake have you made if you tried to read it as a symbol?
exercise_decls.answer: It is the .text symbol’s aux record, not a symbol. You must advance by 1 + NumberOfAuxSymbols slots, so the next real symbol is slot 2
exercise_decls.options: It is the .text symbol’s aux record, not a symbol. You must advance by 1 + NumberOfAuxSymbols slots, so the next real symbol is slot 2|It is a second, unnamed symbol for .text — COFF stores section symbols twice, once with a name and once without|It is the first byte of the aux record, and you have already consumed it as part of .text’s NumberOfAuxSymbols field
exercise_decls.explanation: Slot 0 is the .text symbol with NumberOfAuxSymbols = 1, so it owns slot 1. Reading slot 1 as a symbol shows garbage: the first eight bytes look like a name (6c 00 00 00 03 00 00 00) and its SectionNumber comes out as 0x036c, which is not a section. The rule is: read NumberOfAuxSymbols at offset 17 of each record and advance by 1 + that many slots.
exercise_decls.hint1: Re-read the lesson section 'Check Your Understanding'.
exercise_decls.source_quote: It is the .text symbol’s aux record, not a symbol. You must advance by 1 + NumberOfAuxSymbols slots, so the next real symbol is slot 2

exercise_decls.question: Without looking back: an object's section 4 is named .tls$ and has characteristics 0xc0300040. Section 2 is named .data and has characteristics 0xc0300040. A tool lists a symbol's address as image_base + section.VirtualAddress + symbol.Value, which is correct for every other symbol in the object. What does it report for a thread-local, and where does the information it needs actually live?
exercise_decls.answer: It reports image_base + .tls$.VirtualAddress + symbol.Value, which is an address inside the initial-value template. The offset is correct and is the same in every thread's copy, but the base is a per-thread value the loader supplies through _tls_array and _tls_index, neither of which is knowable offline
exercise_decls.options: It reports image_base + .tls$.VirtualAddress + symbol.Value, which is an address inside the initial-value template. The offset is correct and is the same in every thread's copy, but the base is a per-thread value the loader supplies through _tls_array and _tls_index, neither of which is knowable offline|It reports nothing, because the section is renamed to .tls at load time so the symbol's section number no longer resolves|It correctly reports that the symbol has no static address, because the characteristics show the section is not ordinary data
exercise_decls.explanation: This is the concept in one question. The section header says nothing about TLS, so nothing in the numeric fields tells the tool that section 4 is not ordinary data, and the formula it is applying is exactly the formula that is right everywhere else in the object. So it reports an address inside the section that holds the initial-value template, which is a real address and means nothing at run time. The offset half of the answer is right and is genuinely useful: the symbol's offset within the section is the same in every thread's copy, because the block is copied. The base half is not knowable offline at all, because it comes from _tls_array indexed by a loader-assigned _tls_index, neither of which exists until the program is running. So a tool can report the offset and must not report an address.

exercise_decls.question: Without looking back: an object has a symbol with StorageClass: WeakExternal (0x69), Section: 0, AuxSymbolCount: 1, and an aux record naming symbol 17 as the fallback with Characteristics = 3. Symbol 17 is an absolute symbol named .weak._other_fn.default._call at value 0. No object in the link defines _other_fn. What address does the linker give _other_fn, and what will a program that calls it do?
exercise_decls.answer: It binds to the fallback, so the value is 0 — the address of the synthetic alias symbol. A caller that tests the pointer first takes the fallback path; one that does not test it calls address 0 and crashes
exercise_decls.options: It binds to the fallback, so the value is 0 — the address of the synthetic alias symbol. A caller that tests the pointer first takes the fallback path; one that does not test it calls address 0 and crashes|The linker reports an unresolved external, because a weak reference with no definition is still a reference to nothing|It binds to the nearest library that provides the symbol, and since no object defines it the linker searches the archives and, finding nothing, leaves it at 0
exercise_decls.explanation: The resolution is a substitution: an unresolved weak reference binds to the fallback named in the aux record, so the symbol's value becomes whatever symbol 17 resolves to, which is 0 because it is absolute with no section. The third characteristic is the anti-dependency case, and with no definition anywhere it simply completes as the fallback binds. What the program does next is entirely up to the source, and this is where the concept meets the machine code: because the value is not known at compile time and might be zero, the weak reference compiles to a load, a test and a branch rather than a direct call. A caller that omits the test calls address zero. So the linker doing its job perfectly and the program crashing are not in tension, they are the design working as specified with a caller that skipped the mechanism.
